title: Laws of Chemical Combination & Non-Stoichiometric Exceptions
quickSummary: Classical chemistry establishes five fundamental Laws of Chemical Combination governing matter transformation. At NEST/IChO level, understanding their advanced exceptions (mass defect in nuclear reactions, non-stoichiometric Berthollides like Fe0.95O, and organic polymer limits) is critical.
summary: Master the 5 fundamental laws of chemical combination, their quantitative mathematical formulations, and high-yield NEST exceptions.

summaryBox.title: Core Postulate & Classification
summaryBox.takeaway: Lavoisier (Mass), Proust (Definite), Dalton (Multiple), Richter (Reciprocal), Gay-Lussac (Combining Volumes). Exceptions arise in nuclear physics, non-stoichiometric crystals (Berthollides), and isotopic mixtures.

conceptBreakdown.content:
Matter is anything that possesses mass and occupies space. Classical chemistry establishes five fundamental Laws of Chemical Combination governing chemical transformations:

1. **Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier, 1789)**: In any chemical change, total mass of reactants equals total mass of products (Σ m_reactants = Σ m_products). *Exception*: Nuclear reactions where mass converts to energy (ΔE = Δm·c²).

2. **Law of Definite Proportions (Proust, 1799)**: A pure compound always contains its constituent elements in a fixed ratio by mass (m_A / m_B = Constant). *Exceptions*: Isotopic variation (¹²CO₂ vs ¹⁴CO₂) and Non-Stoichiometric Berthollide compounds (e.g., Fe₀.₉₅O, Cu₁.₈S).

3. **Law of Multiple Proportions (Dalton, 1803)**: When two elements form multiple compounds, masses of element B combining with a fixed mass of A are in simple whole-number ratios (m_B1 : m_B2 = n₁ : n₂). *Exception*: High molecular mass organic polymers (e.g., C₂₀H₄₂ vs C₂₁H₄₄).

4. **Law of Reciprocal Proportions (Richter, 1792)**: The ratio of masses of A and B combining separately with a fixed mass of C is a simple integer multiple of the ratio in which A and B combine directly. *Exception*: When elements exhibit multiple oxidation states with C (e.g., SO₂ vs SO₃).

5. **Gay-Lussac's Law of Combining Volumes (1808)**: Reacting gases combine in simple integer volume ratios at constant T and P. Valid strictly for ideal gases (Z = 1).

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.2 Avogadro's Hypothesis (1811)
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.2 Avogadro's Hypothesis (1811)
conceptBreakdown.content:
Amedeo Avogadro reconciled Dalton's atomic theory with Gay-Lussac's volume law by proposing that equal volumes of all gases under identical conditions of temperature and pressure contain an equal number of molecules:

$$\mathbf{V \propto n \quad (\text{at constant } T, P)}$$

• **Atom**: The smallest particle of an element participating in a chemical reaction; may or may not be capable of independent existence (e.g., He exists independently; O exists as O₂).
• **Molecule**: The smallest particle of an element or compound capable of independent, stable existence.

quickRevision: Law of Conservation of Mass fails in nuclear mass-energy conversions (ΔE = Δm·c²).
Berthollides (Fe0.95O) violate Proust's Law of Definite Proportions.
Avogadro's Law establishes V ∝ n at constant T and P.
